title: Donghak in the 1890s: Religious Mobilization, Rural Grievances, and Reform
description: An editorial introduction to Donghak in the 1890s: Religious Mobilization, Rural Grievances, and Reform, part of the expanding KOREA history archive.

blocks.title: Religion and rural grievances
paragraphs: Donghak linked religious teaching with social concerns in a time of pressure on rural communities and conflict over political legitimacy. Its appeal cannot be explained by one economic cause or by treating all participants as holders of identical beliefs. Religious language could help people express dignity, community, and moral criticism of a social order they experienced as unjust. Regional networks and local leadership helped ideas move beyond the earliest circles of followers.

blocks.title: Organization grew through relationships
paragraphs: Meetings, teachers, shared texts, and practical ties among households could support collective action. The authorities viewed some activities as threats, while adherents interpreted them through different understandings of worship and reform. As conflicts intensified, grievances about officials and social inequality interacted with concerns about foreign influence. The Donghak story is therefore simultaneously religious, social, and political.

blocks.title: From movement to uprising
paragraphs: The path from teaching to large-scale mobilization was not inevitable. Specific disputes, decisions by officials, and local conditions mattered. Accounts written after violent events sometimes read the outcome backward into the origins. Keeping the distinction between earlier religious development and the crises of the 1890s allows readers to follow change without assuming that every believer anticipated war.

blocks.title: Donghak religion and the meaning of political mobilization
paragraphs: Donghak was founded in the nineteenth century by Choe Je-u and developed through religious teaching, networks of adherents and efforts to secure recognition against persecution. Its emphasis on the dignity and spiritual standing of ordinary people made it socially consequential, but it should not be translated mechanically into the political vocabulary of a later constitutional democracy. Followers encountered its teaching through local practice and relationships, not through a single centralized manifesto understood identically everywhere.

The suppression of Choe Je-u and the later movement led by Choe Si-hyeong shaped Donghak's organization. Requests to clear the founder's name and defend the teaching gradually intersected with dissatisfaction about abusive officials and uncertain rural livelihoods. Religious grievance and social protest were therefore intertwined before the armed conflict of 1894. Calling Donghak merely a religious pretext for class rebellion ignores its ethical commitments, while describing it only as worship neglects its ability to mobilize people and challenge public authority.

blocks.title: Rural fiscal burdens as experienced locally
paragraphs: Farmers in late Joseon faced obligations that could include land taxes, military-related exactions, transport work and locally imposed charges. The particular burden varied with landholding, local officials and enforcement practices. An official tax rate tells only part of the story if intermediaries demanded more, records were manipulated, or people could not obtain remedies. Distress was aggravated when households experienced crop uncertainty and debt.

A broad summary of corrupt government can become so vague that it explains nothing. The Gobu complaints associated with Jo Byeong-gap make the problem more concrete: the grievances centred on coercive extraction and the power of a magistrate over local livelihoods. Yet the wider movement cannot be reduced to one abusive official, because participants from several regions recognized comparable problems or sought more ambitious changes. Specific local evidence and the organizing capacity of Donghak networks help explain the expansion.

blocks.title: Petitions, organization and the move toward armed action
paragraphs: Before open revolt, Donghak participants engaged in public petitions and demonstrations that called attention to persecution and demanded recognition. These forms of mobilization connected local adherents and tested how authorities would respond to large gatherings. Communication across villages depended upon trusted organizers and the structures of religious community, especially the network of local jeop and their leaders.

The transformation from petitions to armed resistance was not inevitable. Authorities could respond differently, participants disagreed over tactics, and many people had much to lose in a confrontation with state troops. Escalation requires explaining why existing channels came to appear inadequate for resolving abuse and danger. The first fighting in 1894 emerged from these accumulated tensions rather than suddenly from an abstract revolutionary theory imposed upon the countryside.

blocks.title: A coalition with varying motivations
paragraphs: Donghak adherents and non-adherent farmers could join the same movement without sharing identical religious commitments. Some sought dismissal of corrupt officials or relief from burdens. Others framed their struggle in terms of defending the people and the state from threatening outside influences. Popular assemblies could produce moments of solidarity while preserving disagreements over tactics and ultimate goals.

Jeon Bong-jun's emergence as a leader should be read within this coalition. His significance lay partly in the ability to connect grievances to action and organize forces, not in exercising undisputed command over every participant from the start. Social movements often develop through distributed leadership, even when later history is remembered through famous names. A reconstruction should include the organizational setting that allowed people to respond to calls, gather equipment and take risks together.

blocks.title: Reform demands before the government reforms
paragraphs: The peasant movement's political program challenged abusive administration and elements of inherited status privilege. Its calls for fairness and a government attentive to the common people were not identical to the cabinet-level Gabo reforms later enacted under Japanese military pressure. The two processes overlapped in concerns about old institutions but differed in social base, authority and immediate purpose.

Some reformers at court had debated legal and administrative change for years, while peasant participants demanded accountability from people who exercised power over them. The same policy, such as ending certain privileges, could carry different meanings depending on who demanded it and who enforced it. A comprehensive account must preserve this distinction rather than say that the state simply granted the peasant revolution's program or that external intervention was the sole origin of Korean reform ideas.

blocks.title: The movement on the eve of 1894
paragraphs: By early 1894, local anger, religious connections and experience with collective protest created conditions in which mobilization could spread. The wider international environment heightened concern about Korea's future, but the immediate spark around Gobu remained rooted in local administration. Participants did not know in advance that their uprising would intersect with a war between Qing and Japan or a palace-centered reform movement.

Retrospective history is especially prone to turning beginnings into predictions of endings. The people involved were responding to available information and immediate needs. The first uprising's course, the negotiations around Jeonju and the later resistance to Japanese troops must therefore be narrated as successive choices under changing circumstances. Donghak's religious organization supplied continuity, but the meaning of its political activity changed markedly across the year.
